physical_harm: Six persons were murdered at different places in the house, resulting in death
number_of_offences: Three counts were finally upheld against accused Nos. 1, 3 and 4
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation and planning as the accused had planned the murders and changed clothes to avoid detection
motive: Dispute over the management of the brick-kiln between the accused and deceased Mausam Khan, deceased Shaukeen Khan, and P.W.1
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to the unreliability of the main witnesses and lack of corroboration.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (P.W.1 and P.W.2) as neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable, requiring greater care and corroboration for conviction.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 23rd January, 2014; Trial judgment: 2nd January, 2016; High Court decision: 18th May, 2018; Supreme Court decision: 15th December, 2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Vinod Diwakar, Ms. Nitya Ramakrishnan, Dama Seshadri Naidu, Ms. Shivali Chaudhary, Ananvay Anandvardhan, Siddharth Chapalgaonkar, Ashish Virmani, Anant Agarwal, Ms. Sweta Rani, Ms. Ritika Khanna, Vibhor Jain, Ms. Vinothna V., Advs. for the appearing parties. Counsel for the State: Shri Vinod Diwakar, Additional Advocate General
investigation_status: FIR registered on 23rd January, 2014; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Non-examination of independent witnesses; failure to prove case beyond reasonable doubt; reliance on unreliable witnesses; lack of corroboration; failure to recover bloodstained clothes under Section 27 of the Evidence Act
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and death sentence imposed on accused Nos. 1, 3 and 4; High Court: Acquitted accused No. 2; Supreme Court: Allowed appeals of accused Nos. 1, 3 and 4, dismissed appeal of P.W.1-Ali Sher Khan
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused murdered six deceased at different places in the house, and that the eye-witnesses (P.W.1 and P.W.2) were reliable enough to base a conviction on their testimonies. They also relied on the site-plans, recovery of weapons, and bloodstained clothes as evidence, and claimed that the accused had a motive related to a dispute over the management of the brick-kiln.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the eye-witnesses (P.W.1 and P.W.2) were closely related to the deceased and accused, and therefore their testimonies could not be considered wholly reliable. They also pointed out that the prosecution failed to examine independent witnesses, and that the recovery of weapons and bloodstained clothes lacked credibility. The defence also highlighted inconsistencies in the prosecution's case and the lack of corroboration.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and that the testimony of interested and related witnesses must be scrutinized with due care and caution. The court also emphasized that the burden of proof lies on the prosecution, and that the accused is not required to prove their innocence.
precedent_relied_upon: Vadivelu Thevar & another v. The State of Madras (1957) SCR 981; State of Rajasthan v. Teja Singh and others (2001) 3 SCC 147; Joydeb Patra and others v. State of West Bengal (2014) 12 SCC 444 : [2013] (4) SCR 192; The State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, Baljit Singh and Karam Singh (1974) 3 SCC 277 : [1974] (1) SCR 328; Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala and others (2019) 8 SCC 50 : [2019] (11) SCR 14
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the conviction and death sentence were deemed unsustainable in law.
